titleStmt.title: Indicators and Criteria of Consciousness in Animals and Intelligent Machines: An Inside-Out Approach
titleStmt.author: Pennartz
Farisco
Evers

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Indicators and Criteria of Consciousness in Animals and Intelligent Machines: An Inside-Out Approach

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how to decide which non-human and non-verbal beings possess a property that they cannot report, when no single measurement settles it
span.quote: Instead of proposing criteria that would each define a “hard” threshold for consciousness, we outline six indicators: (i) goal-directed behavior and model-based learning; (ii) anatomic and physiological substrates for generating integrative multimodal representations; (iii) psychometrics and meta-cognition; (iv) episodic memory; (v) susceptibility to illusions and multistable perception; and (vi) specific visuospatial behaviors. Rather than emphasizing a particular indicator as being decisive, we propose that the consistency amongst these indicators can serve to assess consciousness in particular species.

span.label: whether features of conscious experience, which correlate to mechanisms inside the brain, can be logically coupled to externally observable properties
span.quote: Instead of proposing criteria that would each define a “hard” threshold for consciousness, we outline six indicators: (i) goal-directed behavior and model-based learning; (ii) anatomic and physiological substrates for generating integrative multimodal representations; (iii) psychometrics and meta-cognition; (iv) episodic memory; (v) susceptibility to illusions and multistable perception; and (vi) specific visuospatial behaviors. Rather than emphasizing a particular indicator as being decisive, we propose that the consistency amongst these indicators can serve to assess consciousness in particular species.

span.label: six indicators whose CONSISTENCY, rather than any one of which, is used to assess consciousness, integrated into a graded criterion
span.quote: The integration of scores on the various indicators yields an overall, graded criterion for consciousness, somewhat comparable to the Glasgow Coma Scale for unresponsive patients.

span.label: method
span.quote: In this review article, we will suggest operational criteria that can facilitate researchers and policymakers in a range of connected fields of study (neuroscience, AI, psychology and behavioral sciences, medicine, philosophy, ethics and animal welfare) in attributing levels of consciousness to non-verbal beings which may assume varying states of information processing (such as sleep and wakefulness).

span.label: consciousness in non-verbal animals and machines
span.quote: Over the past decades, it has become increasingly important to assess consciousness in non-human and/or non-verbal beings, such as animals and—perhaps in a not too distant future—machines accomplishing sophisticated cognitive tasks.

span.label: review
span.quote: This review article aims to delineate criteria for consciousness especially in animals, while also taking into account intelligent artifacts.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Complex decisions require many variables to be weighed at once, which single-stimulus reflex and habit circuits cannot do; evolution answered this by building brain systems that actively generate rapidly updatable world surveys, and having such a survey is what conscious experience is
span.quote: We suggest that evolution has solved this problem by developing specialized brain systems actively generating rapidly updatable world surveys.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Being fooled by an illusion is possible only if the brain runs an internal model of the causes of sensory input that can, under ambiguity, make perception deviate from the actual generating process - which is why illusion susceptibility indicates conscious, inferential processing
span.quote: Basically, it is impossible to experience an illusion unless the brain harbors an internal model that not only accounts for the causes of a particular pattern of sensory input, but also can cause perception to deviate from the actual process generating sensations, in case of ambiguities in their interpretation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Events must be consciously experienced before they can be stored in declarative memory, so a retrievable episodic trace works backwards as evidence that the original event was experienced consciously
span.quote: Conscious recall is usually understood as being coupled to conscious experiencing of the event before being stored in declarative memory, warranting the proposal that declarative memory and conscious experiencing are tightly and bidirectionally linked to each other

span.label: consciousness HAS A BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION, which is to PRESENT THE SUBJECT WITH A MULTIMODAL, SITUATIONAL SURVEY of the surrounding world and body, subserving complex decision-making - and this survey REFLECTS THE BRAIN'S CAPACITY FOR INTERNAL MODELING of external events
span.quote: We argue that consciousness has a biological function, which is to present the subject with a multimodal, situational survey of the surrounding world and body, subserving complex decision-making and goal-directed behavior. This survey reflects the brain’s capacity for internal modeling of external events underlying changes in sensory state.

span.label: and the choice of construct is justified by what can be measured - volition and voluntary decision-making HAVE BEEN DIFFICULT TO TEST OR QUANTIFY IN PRACTICE, WHEREAS GOAL-DIRECTED BEHAVIOR IS A WELL-DEFINED CONCEPT THAT HAS BEEN OPERATIONALIZED in studies on animal behavior
span.quote: While it has not been uncommon in the past to associate consciousness with volition and voluntary decision-making (Crick and Koch, 2003 ), these latter two concepts have been difficult to test or quantify in practice, whereas goal-directed behavior (see below) is a well-defined concept that has been operationalized in studies on animal behavior (Balleine and Dickinson, 1998 ; Dickinson, 2012 ).

span.label: The article deliberately adopts a narrow, sensory notion of experience and does not defend it against more inclusive views.
span.quote: This points to a limitation in the scope of the current article; we do not theoretically deny the possibility of adopting a more inclusive view on subjective experience (see Farisco et al., 2017 ; Kastrup, 2017 ).

span.label: No proposed indicator constitutes proof of consciousness.
span.quote: First, none of the proposed indicators of consciousness is “hard” in the sense that its satisfaction would offer proof of consciousness.

span.label: Entire taxa are left out of the review because the required evidence is missing.
span.quote: Space is lacking to review indicators of consciousness for amphibians, reptiles and invertebrate species, such as cephalopods and insects, noting that detailed knowledge on the indicators of consciousness reviewed here is often lacking for these species.

span.label: The scheme is still a general heuristic rather than a quantified scale.
span.quote: At the same time, our approach differs from nosological psychiatry because it offers as yet a fairly general heuristic to deal with the problem of consciousness in animals and machines; a concrete and quantitative system (e.g., a linear scale with points) will take more time to develop.

span.label: AN ENTITY MIGHT BE CONSCIOUS EVEN IF IT FAILS TO SATISFY THEM - absence of evidence is not the same as evidence of absence, and at the same time ONE MUST BE CAUTIOUS NOT TO ATTRIBUTE CONSCIOUSNESS TO ANY ARBITRARY OBJECT without further argumentation
span.quote: Such criteria aid us in determining who or what may be conscious, but we must note that an entity might be conscious even if it fails to satisfy them. Like in the neuroimaging assessment of residual consciousness in patients with disorders of consciousness (Schnakers et al., 2009 ; Owen, 2014 ), we should keep in mind here that absence of evidence is not the same as evidence of absence of consciousness. At the same time, one must be cautious not to attribute consciousness to any arbitrary object in nature without further argumentation.

span.label: the approach IS NECESSARILY INDIRECT AND DOES NOT YIELD DEFINITIVE PROOF, BUT RATHER INDICATIONS - an unavoidable consequence of the position that another being's experience is subjective and that knowledge of it IS ALWAYS INFERENTIAL
span.quote: That this approach is necessarily indirect and does not yield definitive proof, but rather indications for consciousness, is an unavoidable consequence of the epistemological position that the conscious experience of other beings, including other humans, is essentially subjective and that relevant knowledge about another subject’s experience is always inferential (Evers and Sigman, 2013 ).

span.label: EACH DEFINITION of a criterion or indicator DEPENDS ON ASSUMPTIONS BEING MADE about what a conscious experience is, how it arises, and what its function may be
span.quote: First and foremost, each definition of a criterion or indicator of consciousness depends on assumptions being made on what a conscious experience is, if and how it normally arises from a brain-body complex interacting with its environment, what its biological function may be, and how it relates to basic computational operations performed by the brain or artificial machinery aiming to replace it, either fully or in part.

span.label: clinical indices have two disadvantages - they MAY BE SPECIFIC TO THE HUMAN BRAIN and may not apply to nervous systems that differ substantially, and THE RANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER WHICH THEY ARE VALID IS INCOMPLETELY KNOWN as they are not derived from a fundamental theory
span.quote: Following up on brain physiology (indicator of consciousness #2), EEG recordings can be utilized in clinical practice to derive the bispectral index, which has been proposed as a measure of awareness vs. depth of anesthesia (for a critical review, see Stein and Glick, 2016 ). Although such indices are useful for evaluating consciousness in humans, they have two significant disadvantages: first, they may be specific to the human brain and may not apply to nervous systems that differ substantially in structure and/or function (e.g., of cephalopods). Second, the range of circumstances under which they are valid is incompletely known as they are not derived from a fundamental theory of consciousness.

span.label: COGNITION DOES NOT ENTAIL CONSCIOUSNESS - cognitive activity inferred via brain activity correlates DOES NOT NECESSARILY CORRESPOND TO CONSCIOUS EXPERIENCE
span.quote: A drawback of this approach is that cognition does not entail consciousness; cognitive activity (inferred via brain activity correlates) does not necessarily correspond to conscious experience (Jox, 2013 ; Peterson et al., 2013 ; Farisco et al., 2015 ).

span.label: for behaviorally unresponsive patients, CURRENTLY NO UNIVERSALLY ACCEPTED CRITERIA ARE AVAILABLE
span.quote: One of the remaining problems is how the conscious status of behaviorally unresponsive patients and other behaviorally incapacitated subjects may be assessed. Currently, no universally accepted criteria are available, but several promising research directions may be indicated.

span.label: and the animal verdict is hedged in the sentence that states it - THIS EVIDENCE IS NOT COMPLETELY UNAMBIGUOUS AND IS CERTAINLY FAR FROM COMPLETE
span.quote: We have reviewed evidence for consciousness in several mammalian and avian species and—although this evidence is not completely unambiguous (and is certainly far from complete)—the force of the combined anatomic, physiological and behavioral-cognitive arguments makes a fairly strong case that rodents and birds do have consciousness. Monkeys make an even stronger case.

span.label: the summed multi-test scoring logic of the Glasgow Coma Scale, imported to grade consciousness across animal species
span.quote: the integration of scores across the various indicators of consciousness can be used as a graded criterion for consciousness, in a similar vein as when unresponsive, brain-damaged patients are subjected to various neurological tests and their scores are summed up to determine the overall grade on the Glasgow Coma Scale (Teasdale et al., 2014 ).

span.label: abductive reasoning (inference to the best explanation) adopted as the method for choosing between competing consciousness theories
span.quote: Again, this approach follows the logic of abductive reasoning, which compares hypotheses and infers the better model based on simplicity, effectiveness and the available evidence (Josephson and Josephson, 1996 ).

span.label: the Glasgow Coma Scale as the model for an integrated, graded score built from several observations rather than one test
span.quote: The integration of scores on the various indicators yields an overall, graded criterion for consciousness, somewhat comparable to the Glasgow Coma Scale for unresponsive patients.

span.label: the rule that a phenomenon may be attributed to a system only where the system displays manifest properties of it, argued through magnetism in iron against plastic
span.quote: As with all phenomena throughout nature, a particular phenomenon X (e.g., magnetism or frozenness) can only be claimed to occur in a system if the system exhibits manifest properties indicating that X is occurring in that system. For instance, iron but not plastic can be said to have magnetic properties because it displays properties of attraction and repulsion in response to an applied magnetic field, even though both iron and plastic are composed of elementary particles obeying the Standard Model of particle physics, which includes electromagnetic interactions. Similarly, consciousness should be attributed only to systems displaying manifest, observable properties such as signs of wakefulness or specific conscious-like behaviors (see “Indicators of Consciousness in Animals” section) or physiological measures (when validated through their tight correlation with other indicators of consciousness). Thus, the validity of theoretically derived measures of consciousness can only be assessed by testing them against other, usually externally observable phenomena that researchers can reasonably agree on as being indicative of consciousness.

span.label: goal-directed behavior as an operationalised construct, imported because volition could not be quantified
span.quote: While it has not been uncommon in the past to associate consciousness with volition and voluntary decision-making (Crick and Koch, 2003 ), these latter two concepts have been difficult to test or quantify in practice, whereas goal-directed behavior (see below) is a well-defined concept that has been operationalized in studies on animal behavior (Balleine and Dickinson, 1998 ; Dickinson, 2012 ).

span.label: prolonged observation across varying circumstances, proposed as the test for machines in place of a single interrogation
span.quote: The rationale is that the evidence for consciousness will optimally accumulate across the study of multiple behaviors (taxing goal-directed behavior, episodic memory, etc.), which should be maintained under varying environmental circumstances (e.g., with novelty, detours) under which stereotypical, pre-programmed solutions can be excluded. Thus, our proposal to assess machine consciousness is as pluralistic as for animals, but more stringent in excluding AI solutions that need not rely on core features of consciousness.

span.label: the requirement that a theoretical measure be tested against phenomena researchers can independently agree on
span.quote: As with all phenomena throughout nature, a particular phenomenon X (e.g., magnetism or frozenness) can only be claimed to occur in a system if the system exhibits manifest properties indicating that X is occurring in that system. For instance, iron but not plastic can be said to have magnetic properties because it displays properties of attraction and repulsion in response to an applied magnetic field, even though both iron and plastic are composed of elementary particles obeying the Standard Model of particle physics, which includes electromagnetic interactions. Similarly, consciousness should be attributed only to systems displaying manifest, observable properties such as signs of wakefulness or specific conscious-like behaviors (see “Indicators of Consciousness in Animals” section) or physiological measures (when validated through their tight correlation with other indicators of consciousness). Thus, the validity of theoretically derived measures of consciousness can only be assessed by testing them against other, usually externally observable phenomena that researchers can reasonably agree on as being indicative of consciousness.

span.label: asking of a theory what would count as disproving it
span.quote: Thus, a problem for IIT is that no criteria are offered to allow to test whether it is correct or incorrect. On the other hand, one could maintain that our “normal” criteria to label entities as conscious have been simply too narrow. This argument holds that IIT offers a fundamental, new law that does not require cross-validation against more conventional ways of conceptualizing consciousness. We believe that this position is flawed because, once again, it would make the theory immune against any form of cross-examination and cross-validation.

span.label: requiring that indicators be compatible with more than one theory of the thing they indicate
span.quote: Which other phenomena, indicative of consciousness, could then be used to test theoretically derived, quantitative measures? Not surprisingly, we refer back to the indicators of consciousness mentioned in “Indicators of Consciousness in Animals” section, noting that they are, on the one hand, linked to the neurorepresentational framework of multimodal, situational survey, but on the other hand are compatible with more than one theory and could thus serve as a more general testbed. Importantly, not only may individual indicators of consciousness provide estimates of conscious state, but especially the consistency amongst scores on different indicators of consciousness can function to provide an overall assessment.

span.label: prolonged ethological observation instead of a single interrogation
span.quote: The rationale is that the evidence for consciousness will optimally accumulate across the study of multiple behaviors (taxing goal-directed behavior, episodic memory, etc.), which should be maintained under varying environmental circumstances (e.g., with novelty, detours) under which stereotypical, pre-programmed solutions can be excluded. Thus, our proposal to assess machine consciousness is as pluralistic as for animals, but more stringent in excluding AI solutions that need not rely on core features of consciousness.

span.label: NO HARD THRESHOLD, SIX INDICATORS, AND THE VERDICT COMES FROM THEIR CONSISTENCY: INSTEAD OF PROPOSING CRITERIA THAT WOULD EACH DEFINE A HARD THRESHOLD, we outline six indicators - and RATHER THAN EMPHASIZING A PARTICULAR INDICATOR AS BEING DECISIVE, THE CONSISTENCY AMONGST THESE INDICATORS CAN SERVE TO ASSESS consciousness
span.quote: Instead of proposing criteria that would each define a “hard” threshold for consciousness, we outline six indicators: (i) goal-directed behavior and model-based learning; (ii) anatomic and physiological substrates for generating integrative multimodal representations; (iii) psychometrics and meta-cognition; (iv) episodic memory; (v) susceptibility to illusions and multistable perception; and (vi) specific visuospatial behaviors. Rather than emphasizing a particular indicator as being decisive, we propose that the consistency amongst these indicators can serve to assess consciousness in particular species.

span.label: with the output a SCORE rather than a verdict: THE INTEGRATION OF SCORES ON THE VARIOUS INDICATORS YIELDS AN OVERALL, GRADED CRITERION, SOMEWHAT COMPARABLE TO THE GLASGOW COMA SCALE for unresponsive patients
span.quote: The integration of scores on the various indicators yields an overall, graded criterion for consciousness, somewhat comparable to the Glasgow Coma Scale for unresponsive patients.

span.label: AND A SINGLE NUMBER IS EXPLICITLY REFUSED AS EVIDENCE: the validity of theoretically derived measures SHOULD NOT BE ASSESSED ON THE BASIS OF A SINGLE QUANTIFIABLE MEASURE, BUT REQUIRES CROSS-EXAMINATION ACROSS MULTIPLE PIECES OF EVIDENCE
span.quote: When considering theoretically derived measures of consciousness, it is argued that their validity should not be assessed on the basis of a single quantifiable measure, but requires cross-examination across multiple pieces of evidence, including the indicators proposed here.

span.label: THE WORD IS CHOSEN TO AVOID A CONNOTATION, AND THE REASON IS GIVEN: many criteria can be best circumscribed as INDICATORS of consciousness, A TERM WHICH AVOIDS THE CONNOTATION OF CRITERION WITH A HARD THRESHOLD in judging whether someone or something is conscious - and OPERATIONAL means SUFFICIENTLY CONCRETE TO APPLY THEM IN THE PRACTICE OF OBSERVING
span.quote: As we will argue, many criteria can be best circumscribed as “indicators of consciousness,” a term which avoids the connotation of “criterion” with a hard threshold in judging or deciding whether someone or something is conscious or not. With “operational” we mean that such indicators of consciousness should be sufficiently concrete to apply them in the practice of observing the behavior or cognitive performance of the subject under scrutiny.

span.label: and a synonym is declared WITH the dissent attached: we will use CONSCIOUSNESS INTERCHANGEABLY WITH AWARENESS, WITHOUT DENYING THAT A DISTINCTION BETWEEN THEM HAS BEEN DRAWN in some previously proposed frameworks
span.quote: We will use the term “consciousness” interchangeably with “awareness,” without denying that a distinction between them has been drawn in some previously proposed frameworks (Farisco et al., 2017 ; Kastrup, 2017 ).

span.label: THE CRITERIA CAN FAIL IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AND THE PAPER SAYS SO IN ITS INTRODUCTION: AN ENTITY MIGHT BE CONSCIOUS EVEN IF IT FAILS TO SATISFY THEM, ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE IS NOT THE SAME AS EVIDENCE OF ABSENCE - and equally, ONE MUST BE CAUTIOUS NOT TO ATTRIBUTE CONSCIOUSNESS TO ANY ARBITRARY OBJECT IN NATURE WITHOUT FURTHER ARGUMENTATION
span.quote: Such criteria aid us in determining who or what may be conscious, but we must note that an entity might be conscious even if it fails to satisfy them. Like in the neuroimaging assessment of residual consciousness in patients with disorders of consciousness (Schnakers et al., 2009 ; Owen, 2014 ), we should keep in mind here that absence of evidence is not the same as evidence of absence of consciousness. At the same time, one must be cautious not to attribute consciousness to any arbitrary object in nature without further argumentation.

span.label: with the epistemic ceiling stated as a consequence rather than a caveat: the approach IS NECESSARILY INDIRECT AND DOES NOT YIELD DEFINITIVE PROOF, BUT RATHER INDICATIONS, because knowledge about another subject's experience IS ALWAYS INFERENTIAL
span.quote: That this approach is necessarily indirect and does not yield definitive proof, but rather indications for consciousness, is an unavoidable consequence of the epistemological position that the conscious experience of other beings, including other humans, is essentially subjective and that relevant knowledge about another subject’s experience is always inferential (Evers and Sigman, 2013 ).

span.label: and every definition is made to declare its own priors: EACH DEFINITION OF A CRITERION OR INDICATOR DEPENDS ON ASSUMPTIONS BEING MADE ON WHAT A CONSCIOUS EXPERIENCE IS, if and how it arises, WHAT ITS BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION MAY BE, and how it relates to basic computational operations
span.quote: First and foremost, each definition of a criterion or indicator of consciousness depends on assumptions being made on what a conscious experience is, if and how it normally arises from a brain-body complex interacting with its environment, what its biological function may be, and how it relates to basic computational operations performed by the brain or artificial machinery aiming to replace it, either fully or in part.

span.label: A MEASURE THAT CANNOT BE CROSS-VALIDATED IS REFUSED: A PROBLEM FOR IIT IS THAT NO CRITERIA ARE OFFERED TO ALLOW TO TEST WHETHER IT IS CORRECT OR INCORRECT - and the defense that it needs no cross-validation IS FLAWED BECAUSE IT WOULD MAKE THE THEORY IMMUNE AGAINST ANY FORM OF CROSS-EXAMINATION
span.quote: Thus, a problem for IIT is that no criteria are offered to allow to test whether it is correct or incorrect. On the other hand, one could maintain that our “normal” criteria to label entities as conscious have been simply too narrow. This argument holds that IIT offers a fundamental, new law that does not require cross-validation against more conventional ways of conceptualizing consciousness. We believe that this position is flawed because, once again, it would make the theory immune against any form of cross-examination and cross-validation.

span.label: with the general principle stated in one sentence, about magnetism: A PARTICULAR PHENOMENON X CAN ONLY BE CLAIMED TO OCCUR IN A SYSTEM IF THE SYSTEM EXHIBITS MANIFEST PROPERTIES INDICATING THAT X IS OCCURRING IN THAT SYSTEM - iron but not plastic can be said to have magnetic properties BECAUSE IT DISPLAYS properties of attraction and repulsion
span.quote: As with all phenomena throughout nature, a particular phenomenon X (e.g., magnetism or frozenness) can only be claimed to occur in a system if the system exhibits manifest properties indicating that X is occurring in that system. For instance, iron but not plastic can be said to have magnetic properties because it displays properties of attraction and repulsion in response to an applied magnetic field, even though both iron and plastic are composed of elementary particles obeying the Standard Model of particle physics, which includes electromagnetic interactions. Similarly, consciousness should be attributed only to systems displaying manifest, observable properties such as signs of wakefulness or specific conscious-like behaviors (see “Indicators of Consciousness in Animals” section) or physiological measures (when validated through their tight correlation with other indicators of consciousness). Thus, the validity of theoretically derived measures of consciousness can only be assessed by testing them against other, usually externally observable phenomena that researchers can reasonably agree on as being indicative of consciousness.

span.label: AND A CATEGORY THAT APPLIES TO EVERYTHING CARRIES NO INFORMATION: the term UNAWARENESS ONLY FINDS LINGUISTIC USE IF IT ARBITRATES BETWEEN CONTRASTING STATES - IF EVERYTHING IN OUR ENVIRONMENT WOULD ALWAYS BE CONSCIOUS, THE CONCEPT WOULD LOSE ITS USEFULNESS IN DAILY OR SCIENTIFIC DISCOURSE
span.quote: Typically, we attribute awareness to systems that may also assume unaware states from time to time, such as deep sleep or anesthesia. This attribution follows the logic that the term “unawareness” only finds linguistic use if it arbitrates between contrasting states or conditions (aware vs. unaware). Even when consciousness would be more multifaceted than hitherto acknowledged, the point remains that, if everything in our environment would always be conscious, the concept would lose its usefulness in daily or scientific discourse (Pennartz, 2015 ).

span.label: and a measure is faulted for having no referent: the quantity DOES NOT REFER TO ANYTHING BEYOND THE SYSTEM'S STATE IT DESCRIBES, it LEAVES THE KEY FEATURE OF INTENTIONALITY UNRESOLVED, and DOES NOT QUANTIFY TO WHAT EXTENT a system GENERATES BELIEFS ABOUT, OR REPRESENTATIONS OF, SOMETHING
span.quote: That IIT is underconstrained as a framework for consciousness raises a second important problem: the quantity it uses to assess consciousness (Φ) does not refer to anything beyond the system’s state it describes. It leaves the key feature of intentionality unresolved, as it does not explain how neural systems can generate contents about something that is different from themselves. In other words, IIT measures do not quantify to what extent a neural (or artificial) system generates beliefs about, or representations of, something.

span.label: with the indicators deliberately built to outlive the theory that proposed them: they are linked to this framework but ARE COMPATIBLE WITH MORE THAN ONE THEORY AND COULD THUS SERVE AS A MORE GENERAL TESTBED
span.quote: Which other phenomena, indicative of consciousness, could then be used to test theoretically derived, quantitative measures? Not surprisingly, we refer back to the indicators of consciousness mentioned in “Indicators of Consciousness in Animals” section, noting that they are, on the one hand, linked to the neurorepresentational framework of multimodal, situational survey, but on the other hand are compatible with more than one theory and could thus serve as a more general testbed. Importantly, not only may individual indicators of consciousness provide estimates of conscious state, but especially the consistency amongst scores on different indicators of consciousness can function to provide an overall assessment.

span.label: AN EXISTING CLINICAL INDEX FAULTED ON TWO GROUNDS: it MAY BE SPECIFIC TO THE HUMAN BRAIN AND MAY NOT APPLY to nervous systems that differ substantially, and THE RANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER WHICH IT IS VALID IS INCOMPLETELY KNOWN AS IT IS NOT DERIVED FROM A FUNDAMENTAL THEORY
span.quote: Following up on brain physiology (indicator of consciousness #2), EEG recordings can be utilized in clinical practice to derive the bispectral index, which has been proposed as a measure of awareness vs. depth of anesthesia (for a critical review, see Stein and Glick, 2016 ). Although such indices are useful for evaluating consciousness in humans, they have two significant disadvantages: first, they may be specific to the human brain and may not apply to nervous systems that differ substantially in structure and/or function (e.g., of cephalopods). Second, the range of circumstances under which they are valid is incompletely known as they are not derived from a fundamental theory of consciousness.

span.label: and a correlate that does not carry the thing: COGNITION DOES NOT ENTAIL CONSCIOUSNESS - cognitive activity, INFERRED VIA BRAIN ACTIVITY CORRELATES, DOES NOT NECESSARILY CORRESPOND TO CONSCIOUS EXPERIENCE
span.quote: A drawback of this approach is that cognition does not entail consciousness; cognitive activity (inferred via brain activity correlates) does not necessarily correspond to conscious experience (Jox, 2013 ; Peterson et al., 2013 ; Farisco et al., 2015 ).

span.label: with the state of the art stated plainly for the hardest case: CURRENTLY NO UNIVERSALLY ACCEPTED CRITERIA ARE AVAILABLE for behaviorally unresponsive patients
span.quote: One of the remaining problems is how the conscious status of behaviorally unresponsive patients and other behaviorally incapacitated subjects may be assessed. Currently, no universally accepted criteria are available, but several promising research directions may be indicated.

span.label: A behavior CAN SATISFY AN INDICATOR WITHOUT THE THING BEING THERE: THERE IS NOTHING IN THE DEFINITION OF GOAL-DIRECTED BEHAVIOR THAT PRECLUDES PRE-PROGRAMMED BEHAVIORS FROM SATISFYING IT - a robot kicks a ball into a goal IN A PRE-PROGRAMMED FASHION AND WILL STEREOTYPICALLY REPEAT ITS ACTION PATTERN
span.quote: The second objection relates to the notion that intelligent robots may be pre-programmed to display goal-directed behavior and other conscious-like behaviors. There is nothing in the definition of goal-directed behavior that precludes pre-programmed behaviors from satisfying it. For instance, a humanoid robot such as Honda’s Asimo (Hirose and Ogawa, 2007 ), on display in Tokyo’s National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation, is capable of kicking a soccer ball into a goal at a distance—which is a remarkable feat of sensorimotor engineering—but it does so in a pre-programmed fashion, and will stereotypically repeat its action pattern on the next show in the same museum.

span.label: and the same indicator may be met by a different route entirely: artificial systems MAY DEVELOP ALTERNATIVE WAYS TO SATISFY BEHAVIORAL INDICATORS by computing solutions IN DIFFERENT WAYS THAN THOSE EVOLVED THROUGH BIOLOGICAL EVOLUTION, so machines COULD DISPLAY SUCH INTELLIGENT, NON-AUTOMATED BEHAVIORS WITHOUT NECESSARILY BEING CONSCIOUS
span.quote: In the future, such artificial systems may develop alternative ways to satisfy behavioral indicators of consciousness by computing solutions for goal-directed behavioral problems, episodic memory, etc., in different ways than those evolved through biological evolution. Instead of attempting to generate a multimodal, situational survey of one’s environment and body, a robot may, for instance, have processors adopting a computational strategy of serial accumulation of evidence, based on a one-by-one scanning of elements in the environment, avoiding the need to construct the kind of overall, integrated survey we would normally consider “conscious.” It remains an open question whether this scenario might result in an alternative kind of consciousness. Whether and how alternative, non-conscious strategies would be effective is unknown, but in principle, it appears possible that intelligent machines could display such intelligent, non-automated behaviors without necessarily being conscious.

span.label: so the test must be longitudinal rather than a snapshot: a different approach is needed THAN A BRIEF TURING-TYPE OF TEST WHICH ONLY PROVIDES A SNAPSHOT of a machine's cognitive capacities OBTAINED BY INTERROGATION, and ADDITIONAL CRITERIA MAY WELL BE NEEDED
span.quote: These considerations accumulate to suggest a different approach to machine consciousness than a brief Turing-type of test which only provides a snapshot of a machine’s cognitive capacities obtained by interrogation. This approach should take into account that machines, having much faster processing units at their disposal, may use other strategies for solving complex problems than relying on conscious surveys of the environment (and are thereby less dependent on the functions of consciousness that apply in a biological context), and may display externally observable indicators such as goal-directed behavior by pre-programmed solutions. Thus, the biological function of consciousness proposed above may thus not be simply transferable upon machines, and additional criteria may well be needed.

span.label: with the rationale for accumulation stated: the evidence WILL OPTIMALLY ACCUMULATE ACROSS THE STUDY OF MULTIPLE BEHAVIORS, MAINTAINED UNDER VARYING ENVIRONMENTAL CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER WHICH STEREOTYPICAL, PRE-PROGRAMMED SOLUTIONS CAN BE EXCLUDED
span.quote: The rationale is that the evidence for consciousness will optimally accumulate across the study of multiple behaviors (taxing goal-directed behavior, episodic memory, etc.), which should be maintained under varying environmental circumstances (e.g., with novelty, detours) under which stereotypical, pre-programmed solutions can be excluded. Thus, our proposal to assess machine consciousness is as pluralistic as for animals, but more stringent in excluding AI solutions that need not rely on core features of consciousness.

span.label: and the current verdict on machines given as a status, not a conclusion: CURRENT INTELLIGENT MACHINES, INCLUDING DEEP LEARNING NEURAL NETWORKS AND AGILE ROBOTS, ARE NOT INDICATED TO BE CONSCIOUS YET
span.quote: Current intelligent machines, including deep learning neural networks (DLNNs) and agile robots, are not indicated to be conscious yet. Instead of assessing machine consciousness by a brief Turing-type of test, evidence for it may gradually accumulate when we study machines ethologically and across time, considering multiple behaviors that require flexibility, improvisation, spontaneous problem-solving and the situational conspectus typically associated with conscious experience.

span.label: THE ANIMAL VERDICT CARRIES ITS OWN HEDGE IN THE SAME SENTENCE: although THIS EVIDENCE IS NOT COMPLETELY UNAMBIGUOUS AND IS CERTAINLY FAR FROM COMPLETE, THE FORCE OF THE COMBINED ANATOMIC, PHYSIOLOGICAL AND BEHAVIORAL-COGNITIVE ARGUMENTS MAKES A FAIRLY STRONG CASE that rodents and birds do have consciousness
span.quote: We have reviewed evidence for consciousness in several mammalian and avian species and—although this evidence is not completely unambiguous (and is certainly far from complete)—the force of the combined anatomic, physiological and behavioral-cognitive arguments makes a fairly strong case that rodents and birds do have consciousness. Monkeys make an even stronger case.

span.quote: As with all phenomena throughout nature, a particular phenomenon X (e.g., magnetism or frozenness) can only be claimed to occur in a system if the system exhibits manifest properties indicating that X is occurring in that system. span.quote: Thus, a problem for IIT is that no criteria are offered to allow to test whether it is correct or incorrect. On the other hand, one could maintain that our “normal” criteria to label entities as conscious have been simply too narrow. This argument holds that IIT offers a fundamental, new law that does not require cross-validation against more conventional ways of conceptualizing consciousness. We believe that this position is flawed because, once again, it would make the theory immune against any form of cross-examination and cross-validation.

span.label: A PARTICULAR PHENOMENON X CAN ONLY BE CLAIMED TO OCCUR IN A SYSTEM IF THE SYSTEM EXHIBITS MANIFEST PROPERTIES INDICATING THAT X IS OCCURRING IN THAT SYSTEM
span.quote: As with all phenomena throughout nature, a particular phenomenon X (e.g., magnetism or frozenness) can only be claimed to occur in a system if the system exhibits manifest properties indicating that X is occurring in that system. For instance, iron but not plastic can be said to have magnetic properties because it displays properties of attraction and repulsion in response to an applied magnetic field, even though both iron and plastic are composed of elementary particles obeying the Standard Model of particle physics, which includes electromagnetic interactions. Similarly, consciousness should be attributed only to systems displaying manifest, observable properties such as signs of wakefulness or specific conscious-like behaviors (see “Indicators of Consciousness in Animals” section) or physiological measures (when validated through their tight correlation with other indicators of consciousness). Thus, the validity of theoretically derived measures of consciousness can only be assessed by testing them against other, usually externally observable phenomena that researchers can reasonably agree on as being indicative of consciousness.

span.label: IF EVERYTHING IN OUR ENVIRONMENT WOULD ALWAYS BE CONSCIOUS, THE CONCEPT WOULD LOSE ITS USEFULNESS IN DAILY OR SCIENTIFIC DISCOURSE
span.quote: Typically, we attribute awareness to systems that may also assume unaware states from time to time, such as deep sleep or anesthesia. This attribution follows the logic that the term “unawareness” only finds linguistic use if it arbitrates between contrasting states or conditions (aware vs. unaware). Even when consciousness would be more multifaceted than hitherto acknowledged, the point remains that, if everything in our environment would always be conscious, the concept would lose its usefulness in daily or scientific discourse (Pennartz, 2015 ).

span.label: the quantity used to assess consciousness DOES NOT REFER TO ANYTHING BEYOND THE SYSTEM'S STATE IT DESCRIBES, and LEAVES THE KEY FEATURE OF INTENTIONALITY UNRESOLVED
span.quote: That IIT is underconstrained as a framework for consciousness raises a second important problem: the quantity it uses to assess consciousness (Φ) does not refer to anything beyond the system’s state it describes. It leaves the key feature of intentionality unresolved, as it does not explain how neural systems can generate contents about something that is different from themselves. In other words, IIT measures do not quantify to what extent a neural (or artificial) system generates beliefs about, or representations of, something.

span.label: the indicators are COMPATIBLE WITH MORE THAN ONE THEORY AND COULD THUS SERVE AS A MORE GENERAL TESTBED
span.quote: Which other phenomena, indicative of consciousness, could then be used to test theoretically derived, quantitative measures? Not surprisingly, we refer back to the indicators of consciousness mentioned in “Indicators of Consciousness in Animals” section, noting that they are, on the one hand, linked to the neurorepresentational framework of multimodal, situational survey, but on the other hand are compatible with more than one theory and could thus serve as a more general testbed. Importantly, not only may individual indicators of consciousness provide estimates of conscious state, but especially the consistency amongst scores on different indicators of consciousness can function to provide an overall assessment.

span.label: clinical indices MAY BE SPECIFIC TO THE HUMAN BRAIN, and THE RANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER WHICH THEY ARE VALID IS INCOMPLETELY KNOWN AS THEY ARE NOT DERIVED FROM A FUNDAMENTAL THEORY
span.quote: Following up on brain physiology (indicator of consciousness #2), EEG recordings can be utilized in clinical practice to derive the bispectral index, which has been proposed as a measure of awareness vs. depth of anesthesia (for a critical review, see Stein and Glick, 2016 ). Although such indices are useful for evaluating consciousness in humans, they have two significant disadvantages: first, they may be specific to the human brain and may not apply to nervous systems that differ substantially in structure and/or function (e.g., of cephalopods). Second, the range of circumstances under which they are valid is incompletely known as they are not derived from a fundamental theory of consciousness.

span.label: COGNITION DOES NOT ENTAIL CONSCIOUSNESS - cognitive activity DOES NOT NECESSARILY CORRESPOND TO CONSCIOUS EXPERIENCE
span.quote: A drawback of this approach is that cognition does not entail consciousness; cognitive activity (inferred via brain activity correlates) does not necessarily correspond to conscious experience (Jox, 2013 ; Peterson et al., 2013 ; Farisco et al., 2015 ).

span.label: CURRENTLY, NO UNIVERSALLY ACCEPTED CRITERIA ARE AVAILABLE for assessing behaviorally unresponsive patients
span.quote: One of the remaining problems is how the conscious status of behaviorally unresponsive patients and other behaviorally incapacitated subjects may be assessed. Currently, no universally accepted criteria are available, but several promising research directions may be indicated.

span.label: THERE IS NOTHING IN THE DEFINITION OF GOAL-DIRECTED BEHAVIOR THAT PRECLUDES PRE-PROGRAMMED BEHAVIORS FROM SATISFYING IT
span.quote: The second objection relates to the notion that intelligent robots may be pre-programmed to display goal-directed behavior and other conscious-like behaviors. There is nothing in the definition of goal-directed behavior that precludes pre-programmed behaviors from satisfying it. For instance, a humanoid robot such as Honda’s Asimo (Hirose and Ogawa, 2007 ), on display in Tokyo’s National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation, is capable of kicking a soccer ball into a goal at a distance—which is a remarkable feat of sensorimotor engineering—but it does so in a pre-programmed fashion, and will stereotypically repeat its action pattern on the next show in the same museum.

span.label: intelligent machines COULD DISPLAY SUCH INTELLIGENT, NON-AUTOMATED BEHAVIORS WITHOUT NECESSARILY BEING CONSCIOUS
span.quote: In the future, such artificial systems may develop alternative ways to satisfy behavioral indicators of consciousness by computing solutions for goal-directed behavioral problems, episodic memory, etc., in different ways than those evolved through biological evolution. Instead of attempting to generate a multimodal, situational survey of one’s environment and body, a robot may, for instance, have processors adopting a computational strategy of serial accumulation of evidence, based on a one-by-one scanning of elements in the environment, avoiding the need to construct the kind of overall, integrated survey we would normally consider “conscious.” It remains an open question whether this scenario might result in an alternative kind of consciousness. Whether and how alternative, non-conscious strategies would be effective is unknown, but in principle, it appears possible that intelligent machines could display such intelligent, non-automated behaviors without necessarily being conscious.

span.label: a different approach is needed THAN A BRIEF TURING-TYPE OF TEST WHICH ONLY PROVIDES A SNAPSHOT of a machine's cognitive capacities
span.quote: These considerations accumulate to suggest a different approach to machine consciousness than a brief Turing-type of test which only provides a snapshot of a machine’s cognitive capacities obtained by interrogation. This approach should take into account that machines, having much faster processing units at their disposal, may use other strategies for solving complex problems than relying on conscious surveys of the environment (and are thereby less dependent on the functions of consciousness that apply in a biological context), and may display externally observable indicators such as goal-directed behavior by pre-programmed solutions. Thus, the biological function of consciousness proposed above may thus not be simply transferable upon machines, and additional criteria may well be needed.

span.label: CURRENT INTELLIGENT MACHINES, INCLUDING DEEP LEARNING NEURAL NETWORKS AND AGILE ROBOTS, ARE NOT INDICATED TO BE CONSCIOUS YET
span.quote: Current intelligent machines, including deep learning neural networks (DLNNs) and agile robots, are not indicated to be conscious yet. Instead of assessing machine consciousness by a brief Turing-type of test, evidence for it may gradually accumulate when we study machines ethologically and across time, considering multiple behaviors that require flexibility, improvisation, spontaneous problem-solving and the situational conspectus typically associated with conscious experience.

span.label: although THIS EVIDENCE IS NOT COMPLETELY UNAMBIGUOUS AND IS CERTAINLY FAR FROM COMPLETE, the combined arguments MAKE A FAIRLY STRONG CASE THAT RODENTS AND BIRDS DO HAVE CONSCIOUSNESS
span.quote: We have reviewed evidence for consciousness in several mammalian and avian species and—although this evidence is not completely unambiguous (and is certainly far from complete)—the force of the combined anatomic, physiological and behavioral-cognitive arguments makes a fairly strong case that rodents and birds do have consciousness. Monkeys make an even stronger case.

span.label: indicators of consciousness
span.quote: As we will argue, many criteria can be best circumscribed as “indicators of consciousness,” a term which avoids the connotation of “criterion” with a hard threshold in judging or deciding whether someone or something is conscious or not.

span.label: operational (as applied to indicators)
span.quote: With “operational” we mean that such indicators of consciousness should be sufficiently concrete to apply them in the practice of observing the behavior or cognitive performance of the subject under scrutiny.

span.label: inside-out approach
span.quote: The term “inside-out approach” does not entail that the contents of experience are internally situated (i.e., within the brain) but refers to the localization of neural mechanisms underlying experience inside the brain.

span.label: qualitative richness
span.quote: Qualitative richness Conscious experience is specified by a wide, varied palette of sensory modalities and submodalities

span.label: situatedness
span.quote: Situatedness Conscious experience is set in a specific spatiotemporal situation in which the subject is immersed

span.label: intentionality
span.quote: Intentionality Conscious experience is about something other than is entailed by the underlying neuronal substrates; it depends on the subjective interpretation of external or internal inputs to the brain

span.label: integration
span.quote: Integration The elements of a scene or situation we perceive are experienced as a unified whole

span.label: dynamics and stability
span.quote: Dynamics and stability Brain systems for conscious processing allow for both dynamic changes in experience as well as short-term stabilization of percepts

span.label: goal-directed behavior
span.quote: Agents display goal-directed behavior when this behavior is driven by a representation of the expected consequences of action and depends on knowledge of actions being causal for obtaining a desirable outcome (Dickinson, 2012 ).

span.label: model-based learning
span.quote: Model-based learning is defined by the subject building an explicit, internal model of its state space, including specific stimulus–outcome relationships and enabling prospective cognition and on-the-fly decision-making

span.label: episodic memory
span.quote: This type of memory is defined as autobiographical memory, that is memory of events (“what”) a subject experienced at a particular place (“where”) and time (“when”).

span.label: conscious-like behavior
span.quote: we propose the term “conscious-like behavior” as a summary term for animals displaying consistently positive scores on behavioral indicators of consciousness.

span.label: indicator
span.quote: As we will argue, many criteria can be best circumscribed as “indicators of consciousness,” a term which avoids the connotation of “criterion” with a hard threshold in judging or deciding whether someone or something is conscious or not. With “operational” we mean that such indicators of consciousness should be sufficiently concrete to apply them in the practice of observing the behavior or cognitive performance of the subject under scrutiny.

span.label: consciousness
span.quote: We argue that consciousness has a biological function, which is to present the subject with a multimodal, situational survey of the surrounding world and body, subserving complex decision-making and goal-directed behavior. This survey reflects the brain’s capacity for internal modeling of external events underlying changes in sensory state.

span.label: awareness
span.quote: We will use the term “consciousness” interchangeably with “awareness,” without denying that a distinction between them has been drawn in some previously proposed frameworks (Farisco et al., 2017 ; Kastrup, 2017 ).

span.label: six — number of indicators of consciousness the authors propose in place of hard-threshold criteria
span.quote: Instead of proposing criteria that would each define a “hard” threshold for consciousness, we outline six indicators: (i) goal-directed behavior and model-based learning; (ii) anatomic and physiological substrates for generating integrative multimodal representations; (iii) psychometrics and meta-cognition; (iv) episodic memory; (v) susceptibility to illusions and multistable perception; and (vi) specific visuospatial behaviors.

span.label: six indicators — the number of separate observable properties whose CONSISTENCY, not any one of which, is read as evidence
span.quote: Instead of proposing criteria that would each define a “hard” threshold for consciousness, we outline six indicators: (i) goal-directed behavior and model-based learning; (ii) anatomic and physiological substrates for generating integrative multimodal representations; (iii) psychometrics and meta-cognition; (iv) episodic memory; (v) susceptibility to illusions and multistable perception; and (vi) specific visuospatial behaviors. Rather than emphasizing a particular indicator as being decisive, we propose that the consistency amongst these indicators can serve to assess consciousness in particular species.

span.label: indicator
span.quote: Which other phenomena, indicative of consciousness, could then be used to test theoretically derived, quantitative measures? Not surprisingly, we refer back to the indicators of consciousness mentioned in “Indicators of Consciousness in Animals” section, noting that they are, on the one hand, linked to the neurorepresentational framework of multimodal, situational survey, but on the other hand are compatible with more than one theory and could thus serve as a more general testbed. Importantly, not only may individual indicators of consciousness provide estimates of conscious state, but especially the consistency amongst scores on different indicators of consciousness can function to provide an overall assessment.

span.label: measure
span.quote: When considering theoretically derived measures of consciousness, it is argued that their validity should not be assessed on the basis of a single quantifiable measure, but requires cross-examination across multiple pieces of evidence, including the indicators proposed here.
